newsitem.title: POLAND: PRIME MINISTER BRACES POLAND FOR MORE FLOODS.
newsitem.headline: PRIME MINISTER BRACES POLAND FOR MORE FLOODS.

text.p: Poland's Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz on Friday braced his country for more possible flooding this weekend, saying the government would do all it could do compensate victims from loss.
"We have to go forward, we have to think about in what way we can remove the effects of the cataclysm," Cimoszewicz said in a televised addresss after the evening news.
"On the proposal of the government more than 30 laws have been amended -- all so that aid should reach you quickly and without unnecessary bureaucratic procedures," he added.

On Thursday night Parliament passed the laws to allow the government to increase borrowing and to rush both funds and aid to smitten areas. In the early hours, President Aleksander Kwasniewski announced he had signed them into law.
The parliament also hastily amended the communist-era state of emergency law, cutting its most undemocratic provisions, so it could be applied in case of a new round of the calamity.

On Friday evening Kwasniewski, visiting badly afflicted areas in the southeastern Tarnobrzeg province, said he would sign the amended law but for the time being had no intention to call a state of emergency, PAP news agency reported .
Kwasniewski said earlier in the day that a declaration of a state of emergency would delay September 21 parliamentary elections and for the time being was unnecessary.
Poland's official crisis committee said that renewed floods were on the way after rain fell throughout Friday on the western third of a country already mourning 48 deaths in the two-week calamity.
Committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes said it was hard to say on what scale the flooding would be but that effects might be evident in the next hours.
Pomes said the rain was lighter than downpours two weeks ago which unleashed the region's worst natural disaster in centuries, but the ground was soaked and reservoirs full.
But he said this time Poles were better prepared with evacuation plans and flood defences.
